lesson.title: Strong Verbs & Ancient Ablaut
lesson.subtitle: sing/sang/sung ↔ singen/sang/gesungen — the vowel melody, not endings

hook.title: The Vowel Melody
hook.content: English never announces its irregular verbs with endings — it changes the VOWEL: sing, sang, sung. drink, drank, drunk. So does German, with the exact same vowels: singen, sang, gesungen. trinken, trank, getrunken. This is ablaut — the ancient Indo-European system of grading the root vowel — and it is the strongest proof of siblinghood in the entire language: nobody learns sing/sang/sung from a rule; both languages inherited the melody whole. The lesson is not memorization. It is hearing that you already know the tune.

footnotes.title: Strong Does Not Mean Difficult
footnotes.content: 'Strong' verbs (starke Verben) are the old Germanic verbs that form the past by vowel change; 'weak' verbs are the newer ones that added a -t/-te ending (English's -ed). The strong ones are a closed club — no new members — and you already belong: sing, drink, find, give, speak, come, take are all ancient members, and each has its German twin inside.

pattern.title: Hear the Family, Then the Class
pattern.content: The e→i / a / o families: geben, gab, gegeben ↔ give, gave, given. sprechen, sprach, gesprochen ↔ speak, spoke, spoken. nehmen, nahm, genommen — its melody matches come/came (nehmen's true English twin is archaic nim, the word inside nimble). The a-families: finden, fand, gefunden ↔ find, found — the same class again. trinken, trank, getrunken ↔ drink, drank, drunk, vowel for vowel. The long families: fahren, fuhr, gefahren ↔ fare, fared — and schreiben, schrieb, geschrieben, the scribe family with its own strong melody. Every strong verb you own in English has a German twin singing the same three notes.
pattern.linguist_note: The classes go back to seven Proto-Germanic Ablaut classes (Wright's grammar catalogs them all). You do not need the numbering — you need the reflex: strong past = change the vowel, and ge- + -en for the participle (getrunken, geschrieben, gefahren).

exercises.prompt: Match each English ablaut melody with its German twin. Then recall earlier vocabulary in the short phrases:
exercises.target_answer: singen / sang / gesungen, trinken / trank / getrunken, finden / fand, geben / gab / gegeben, blasen / blies / geblasen, frieren / fror / gefroren, Wir können fliegen
exercises.meaning: sing / sang / sung; drink / drank / drunk; find / found; give / gave / given; blow / blew / blown; freeze / froze / frozen; We can fly
exercises.explanation: The same three-note melody in both languages — ablaut is shared inheritance, not coincidence.

exercises.prompt: Separate the one different connection from this small review set.
exercises.meaning: Recognize a familiar German word by choosing between earlier connection patterns.
exercises.explanation: Table, deep and drink share D → T. Brother → Bruder uses TH → D.
Strong participle: ge- + changed vowel + -en. fand's vowel u-pops into gefunden — exactly like found's ou.

exercises.prompt: English for Gib ihm das Buch — pick every shape that really says it:
exercises.target_answer: Give him the book, Give the book to him
exercises.explanation: English says the same thought three ways and drops the 'to' in all of them. German never drops it — ihm *is* 'to him', in the dative's own shape. That is why German sounds like the word-for-word version: German kept the construction English quietly discarded.
exercises.affirmation: All three natural shapes, neither literal one — you matched the thought, not the word order.

exercises.idea: you've been looking everywhere for the book — and you can finally announce: you have found the book
idea_parts: the strong participle → gefunden, parked at the end
cues: Strong verb, three notes: finden, fand, gefunden — the melody's third note closes the bracket
exercises.affirmation: You kept the melody's third note — gefunden closes the bracket the way sung closes 'have sung'.
exercises.explanation: Strong participle gefunden closes the Perfekt bracket: 'habe' opens, the melody's third note lands last.

summary.outcome: Recognize the shared ablaut melodies and form strong pasts and participles.
summary.takeaway: Strong verbs change the root vowel — sing/sang ↔ singen/sang — and wear ge- + -en as participles.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: sing/sang/sung Mirrors — practise German Ablaut forms with English memory clues.

twist.prompt: Now ask it: you have found the book → HAVE you found the book? (The helper flips to position 1.)
twist.explanation: In a question the helper haben takes position 1 and the subject follows — the participle still closes the bracket. Hast is the thou-form: 'Hast thou...?' was English once.

singen.etymology_derivation: Initial S voiced to [z] before vowels.

trinken.context_translation: I drink a glass of water.

finden.context_translation: I cannot find it / I find it not.
finden.etymology_derivation: Stem find + infinitive -en (German keeps pure short [ɪ] vowel).

geben.context_translation: There is a problem (literally: it gives a problem).
geben.etymology_derivation: v → b. In impersonal form "es gibt", expresses existence.

nehmen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *nemaną — the twin of archaic English nim 'to take', surviving in nimble ('quick to grasp'); English take is a Norse import. [wiktionary]

fahren.context_translation: I am going / driving to Berlin.
fahren.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *faraną — the twin of English fare (farewell, bus fare, 'how did you fare?'). [wiktionary]

schreiben.etymology_derivation: A Latin loan (scribere) that both languages Germanicized — English kept it in scribe, script, describe. Strong verb: schrieb, geschrieben. [wiktionary]

schlafen.etymology_derivation: p → f with sl- → schl- cluster.

blasen.context_translation: The wind is blowing hard today.
blasen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *blāsan, a class 7 strong verb (blies, geblasen); the fetched page gives no English cognate, but the standard twin is English blow (blew, blown). [UNVERIFIED — check] [wiktionary]

frieren.context_translation: Are you cold? I am making tea.
frieren.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *freusaną — the page names English freeze as a cognate; the strong past fror, gefroren mirrors froze, frozen. The German infinitive r spread from the old past forms. [wiktionary]

tragen.etymology_derivation: Class 6 strong verb from Proto-Germanic *draganą (to carry, drag) - the twin of English draw and drag; tragen-trug-getragen matches draw-drew-drawn. [wiktionary]

fliegen.context_translation: We are flying to Rome tomorrow.
fliegen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *fleuganą (PIE *plewk-) — English fly is the documented cognate; strong verb: flog, geflogen. [wiktionary]

bäckerei.etymology_derivation: Bäcker (baker, from backen — English bake) + -ei, the place suffix: the bake-house. [wiktionary]

wunde.context_phrase: Die Wunde am Bein heilt gut.
wunde.context_translation: The wound on the leg is healing well.
wunde.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *wundō, from *wundaz, wounded; the page lists English wound as cognate — the same wound-word carried sound-alike into both languages. [wiktionary]

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: English and German share the 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels rather than adding endings.
strong_verbs_ablaut.philological_note: Joseph Wright's Historical German Grammar categorizes these 7 classes. Knowing "sing-sang-sung" gives you "singen-sang-gesungen", "drink-drank-drunk" gives you "trinken-trank-getrunken", and "drive-drove-driven" gives you "treiben-trieb-getrieben".
